statement: The marginal distribution of a subset of random variables (here X, from a pair (X,Y)) is obtained from their joint distribution by eliminating (marginalizing out) the other variable(s) Y: sum the joint pmf over all values of Y (discrete case) or integrate the joint pdf over Y (continuous case).

symbols.meaning: random variables with a known joint distribution
joint probability mass function of X and Y
joint probability density function of X and Y
conditional pmf/pdf of X given Y=y
expectation taken over the distribution of Y
collection of random variables with a joint distribution

steps.text: Start from the known joint distribution of X and Y: discrete case p(x_i, y_j); continuous case f(x,y). This encodes the probability of X and Y taking values together, without yet discarding either variable.

Marginalize out Y by summing (discrete) or integrating (continuous) the joint distribution over every value Y can take, discarding Y's identity: p_X(x_i) = \sum_j p(x_i, y_j), and symmetrically p_Y(y_j) = \sum_i p(x_i, y_j); for continuous variables f_X(x) = \int_c^d f(x,y)\,dy and f_Y(y) = \int_a^b f(x,y)\,dx. This is literally 'summing values in a table along rows or columns and writing the sum in the margins.'

Rewrite the marginalization integral as a conditional expectation. Substitute the definition of the conditional distribution, p_{X,Y}(x,y) = p_{X|Y}(x|y)\,p_Y(y), into the integral from Step 2: p_X(x) = \int_y p_{X|Y}(x|y)\,p_Y(y)\,dy. By the law of the unconscious statistician, E_Y[f(Y)] = \int_y f(y)\,p_Y(y)\,dy, this integral is exactly E_Y[p_{X|Y}(x|Y)]. So marginalizing X is equivalent to averaging the conditional probability of X over all values of Y, weighted by how likely each value of Y is.

As a special case, this expectation form gives the transformation rule for a deterministic function X = g(Y): since p_{X|Y}(x|y) = \delta(x - g(y)), Step 3 becomes p_X(x) = \int_y \delta(x - g(y))\,p_Y(y)\,dy.

Obtain the marginal CDF the same way, by evaluating the joint CDF at the edge of Y's support rather than integrating a density: if X, Y jointly take values on [a,b]\times[c,d], then F_X(x) = F(x,d) and F_Y(y) = F(b,y); if the support is unbounded, F_X(x) = \lim_{y\to\infty} F(x,y).

Generalize to n jointly distributed variables X_1,\dots,X_n: the marginal of a single X_i is obtained by summing (discrete) or integrating (continuous) the joint pmf/pdf over every other variable, p_{X_i}(k) = \sum p(x_1,\dots,x_{i-1},k,x_{i+1},\dots,x_n), and analogously with an (n-1)-fold integral for the continuous pdf f_{X_i}(x_i).

assumptions.assumption: The full joint distribution over all variables (including the ones to be discarded) is known.
assumptions.breaks_when: Only a conditional or partial distribution is available; then the sum/integral in Step 2 cannot be formed.

assumptions.assumption: The sum (discrete) or integral (continuous) over the discarded variable's entire support converges/exists.
assumptions.breaks_when: The joint pmf/pdf is not summable or integrable over Y, e.g. an improper density with divergent tails.

failure_modes.signature: Reported probability of X ignores that it was implicitly computed only for one value or a restricted range of Y
failure_modes.cause: Summing/integrating over an incomplete set of Y values (Step 2) instead of the full support of Y, e.g. treating a subset of a table as if it were the whole margin

failure_modes.signature: The integral in Step 2 diverges or the sum has no finite value
failure_modes.cause: Joint density not integrable over Y's support, violating the convergence assumption above

failure_modes.mode: Wrong marginal CDF at finite bounds
failure_modes.signature: F_X(x) computed from F(x, y) at some finite y instead of the true upper bound d (or the limit as y\to\infty)
failure_modes.cause: Step 5 applied with the wrong edge of Y's support instead of its supremum
